extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) prosecuting AI-related patent applications before the USPTO and PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and prosecuting patent applications directed to AI/ML inventions, including how to avoid/overcome §101 and §112 rejections and handle PTAB practice. Focuses on specification content, claim drafting, and response strategies tailored for AI technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/Solution Description
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a description of a technical problem, the technical solution, and the resulting improvement over related technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a field of technology, give a generic name for a device/task, and describe a problem faced when implementing such a task or device without conceding too much background as prior art. Describe structure performing each function recited in the claims; if implemented in software, provide an algorithm for how the function is performed. If an AI-specific term is claimed, provide a non-limiting definition or an exemplary use in the specification. Preferably show how the technical solution results in an improvement specific to a particular area of technology and tied directly to the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to §101: Three key strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: When responding to a Section 101 rejection, pursue one or more of three strategies: (1) argue the claim does not recite a judicial exception; (2) argue the claim is integrated into a practical application; (3) argue additional elements (or their combination) add significantly more than conventional solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These strategies map to steps 2–4 of the eligibility test. Prepare arguments tailored to each prong and support them with specification detail and claim amendments as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for the four-step subject-matter-eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate and prepare arguments for steps: (1) statutory category; (2) whether claims recite an abstract idea; (3) whether the claim is integrated into a practical application; (4) whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember examiners must go through all steps (unless rejected at step 1). Structure claim and specification content to address each step explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid language reciting a mental process or show impracticality for human mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental process rejections are common for AI claims; avoid claim language that sounds like mental processes or demonstrate that limitations cannot practically be performed mentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change verbs like 'predict' to 'compute' or add architecture-specific elements that cannot be performed mentally (e.g., 'performing a convolution on an image', 'generating an embedding vector'). Explicitly describe computational complexity (e.g., training takes a month on a supercomputer) and state steps are 'impractical' to perform in the human mind. Note: 'impractical' is distinct from merely 'inconvenient' or 'faster with a computer'—convenience/speed alone will not save a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend claim language to add architecture-specific elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Overcome mental-process and abstract-idea concerns by reciting specific architectural elements or concrete computational steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite details such as particular layer types (self-attention layers, U-nets), specific activation functions, or concrete operations (convolutions, embedding generation) rather than generic terms ('ML model', 'neural network') to show the claim is not merely a mental process or abstract concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe computational complexity in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Document in the specification that claimed elements are computationally intensive or complex to demonstrate impracticality of human performance and support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claim steps that take substantial compute (e.g., month-long training on a supercomputer) or that are 'computationally intensive/complex' as described in the specification will support arguments against mental process rejections and show technical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking 'methods of organizing human behavior' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that explicitly recite activities in the enumerated sub-categories (fundamental economic practices, commercial/legal interactions, managing personal behavior/relationships) are vulnerable to this abstract-idea grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, draft claims to focus on processes performed directly by the AI model (computing vectors, transforming text/images) rather than the ultimate human-facing objective (e.g., creating a legal agreement). Avoid terms like 'contract document' when not necessary, since such language can invite a legal-interaction characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid explicitly reciting mathematical formulas; claim descriptive technical specifics instead
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concept rejections are less common but risky if claims recite formulas; claims need not recite algorithms or formulas to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For training claims, recite elements of a loss function descriptively rather than the exact formula. For inferencing claims, claim specifics of input data, the transformation to the data, specifics of output data, and data-preparation steps rather than mathematical operations. For model architecture claims, recite particular types of layers and their functions without reciting low-level mathematical operations (dot products, summations) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim specific structures rather than generic computer components
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims stating use of 'a processor' and 'memory' or generic 'ML model' will likely draw §101 rejections under step 3 (2A Prong 2) for relying on generic computer components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite more specific architectural elements (specific layer types, sensor inputs, data structures) and describe corresponding implementation details in the specification to avoid being considered 'generic computer components.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include improvements to computer/ML functioning and technical transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that show an improvement to the functioning of a computer or ML model, or that effect a transformation of a particular article to a different state, support arguments that claims are integrated into a practical application or amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of persuasive limitations: improve functioning of a computer or ML model; implement judicial exception with a particular machine; include elements that perform claimed steps concretely; effect a transformation of a particular thing (e.g., transform images/documents/audio). Tie the improvement directly to the technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the judicial exception in a meaningful, technology-specific way
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely linking an abstract idea to a technological environment is insufficient; claims should include technical elements that meaningfully link the judicial exception to the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite sensor-specific data, environment-unique outputs, architectural or procedural steps that are specific to the technological environment. Show how ordered tokens/embeddings or other ML specifics are rooted in the technical domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combinations of additional elements and unconventional solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy step 4 (2B), emphasize unconventional elements or non-routine combinations that, when taken together, amount to an inventive concept significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if some elements might be judicial exceptions alone, show how unconventional combinations integrate into a practical application. Explicitly point out combinations in response to rejections and cite specification passages that demonstrate unconventionality. Note examiners must provide evidence if asserting elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate unconventional mathematical techniques where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconventional mathematical techniques can be relevant additional elements in the §101 2B analysis when they are part of a novel combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if mathematical in nature, include and emphasize unconventional mathematical/algorithmic steps in the specification and claims, and explain how they contribute to a technological improvement when combined with other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft training claims with sufficient specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Training claims that are drafted at a high level of generality are increasingly being rejected under §101; training claims should be detailed to demonstrate technical improvement and avoid abstract-idea characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model training claims should include specifics about data transformations, stages of training, structure of training sets, particular model architectures, and concrete improvements in model functioning or computing. Use the same considerations used for other AI claims to show practical application and technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (§112(a)): disclose computer and algorithm details
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented functional claims, the specification should disclose the computer and the algorithm (necessary steps and/or flowcharts) that perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an identification of the structure performing each claimed function, a description of an algorithm (finite sequence of steps, flowcharts), details of structural elements used to perform the function, and descriptions of how exceptions are handled. Use the three recommended levels of architecture/training description to support enablement and written description arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement perspective: consider the PHOSITA standard in a fast-moving field
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 requirements should be evaluated from the perspective of a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA), which may differ from the inventors' expertise in fast-moving AI fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between what an ordinary practitioner in AI would understand and the inventors' specialized knowledge; include sufficient disclosure to bring PHOSITA to the claimed invention without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness (§112(b)) and avoid means-plus-function pitfalls (§112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularity and definiteness require proper antecedent basis and avoiding generic functional claim language that could be construed as means-plus-function without corresponding structure in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid informalities like missing antecedent basis. For every claimed function, identify structure performing it and include corresponding structural/algorithmic disclosure to prevent the claim being interpreted under §112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'black box' descriptions; disclose implementation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing computer parts or ML components as 'black boxes' risks findings that the disclosure is insufficient and that claimed elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed disclosure of computer hardware, functional requirements, and detailed flow charts or routines for performing claimed steps. Lack of detail can lead to PTAB or Examiner conclusions that details are conventional and thus not 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue claim-by-claim and avoid representative-claim pitfalls on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB may select a single claim as exemplary if applicants fail to provide separate arguments for different claim types, which can render all claims vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present separate arguments for method, apparatus, and program claims with respect to judicial exception analyses to prevent PTAB from deciding the appeal based on a single representative claim; burden is on applicant to argue patentability of each claim type separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on PTAB/precedential decisions carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may refuse to consider PTAB decisions unless designated as precedential or informative; there are few such decisions for AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer citing decisions designated as precedential or informative where possible (e.g., Ex parte Hannun was designated informative). When citing other decisions, be prepared to justify relevance and to tie the decision’s facts closely to your case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity matters: claim-level detail can distinguish eligible from ineligible examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of specificity in claim limitations often determines eligibility: detailed technical steps are more likely to be seen as non-abstract than high-level 'collecting/analyzing/displaying' recitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the MPEP examples as guidance: claims detailing GPS pseudo-range calculations, network packet analysis, specific encryption methods, or pixel-wise halftoning are examples of claims that do not recite mental processes/mathematical concepts, whereas broad data-collection/analysis/display claims are problematic. Emphasize concrete data structures and manipulations.
